title: How a Nurse’s Super-Smell Detects Parkinson’s Disease Early: Joy Milne’s Breakthrough
summary:
Joy Milne, a nurse with hereditary hyperosmia—a heightened sense of smell—discovered she could detect Parkinson’s disease through a distinct odor years before medical science caught up. Her extraordinary ability, first noticed in her husband Les at age 31, later led to groundbreaking research proving that Parkinson’s alters sebum composition, producing a unique volatile signature detectable by trained noses or advanced GCMS machines. This discovery has since transformed into a non-invasive diagnostic test, offering hope for earlier intervention in a disease that typically remains undiagnosed until 50% of neural damage has already occurred.

Milne’s journey began in 1956 when her grandmother revealed her heightened olfactory sensitivity, which she later termed her "nursing bag of smells." By the 1980s, she noticed Les’s musky scent changing subtly, a shift that preceded his Parkinson’s diagnosis by 12 years. In 2012, Milne’s observation at a Parkinson’s UK meeting confirmed her ability to distinguish patients by smell alone. Collaborating with researchers like Dr. Thilo Kunath and Professor Perdita Barran, she validated her findings through a 2019 study where she correctly identified Parkinson’s in 12 out of 12 participants using T-shirt samples, with one false positive later confirmed as a pre-diagnosis case. Today, her work with Nose to Diagnose has led to a simple five-minute swab test, now being translated for global use in hospitals.

title: How Tech Brands Manipulate Specs and Why You Should Ignore Their Claims
tags: up to claims in tech specs
summary:
Tech giants like Apple, Samsung, and Rivian have weaponized vague language and misleading metrics to sell incremental upgrades as revolutionary breakthroughs. In this eye-opening collaboration with Marques Brownlee (MKBHD), the video exposes how phrases like "up to 2x faster" or "world’s first 140x zoom" are designed to obscure reality rather than inform consumers. Watch the full breakdown above to see how these tactics manipulate your purchasing decisions.

The core deception lies in three pervasive strategies: invented specs, exaggerated performance claims, and selective comparisons. Companies like Apple redefine RAM as "unified memory" to obscure the fact that shared memory pools limit multitasking, while EV makers like Rivian combine maximum range with minimum prices in impossible configurations. Even fundamental measurements like "1-inch camera sensors" or "1.5K displays" are repurposed marketing terms divorced from their technical meanings. The video also reveals how tech brands compare new chips to decade-old models to inflate performance gains, and how screen brightness or zoom claims often prioritize peak numbers over real-world usability. These tactics aren’t just misleading—they’re calculated to make you upgrade more frequently by obscuring incremental improvements.

title: Why Yartsa Gunbu Fungus Costs Thousands Per Pound
tags: most expensive fungus in the world
summary:
The parasitic fungus *Ophiocordyceps sinensis*—infamously known as Yartsa Gunbu—is one of the most lucrative and sought-after organisms on Earth, with a single pound fetching tens of thousands of dollars in global markets. This bizarre yet fascinating organism begins its life cycle as a ghost moth caterpillar, which unwittingly becomes a host for the fungus after spores infect it underground. PBS NOVA’s *Gross Science* series reveals how this parasitic relationship transforms the caterpillar into a biological incubator, ultimately sprouting a brown fungal stalk from its head to spread spores and perpetuate the cycle. Watch the embedded video above to witness this macabre yet mesmerizing process unfold.

The video exposes the parasitic mechanism behind Yartsa Gunbu’s formation, detailing how the fungus infiltrates a caterpillar’s body, consumes its organs from within, and manipulates its behavior to crawl near the soil’s surface before killing it. In spring, the fungus erupts from the caterpillar’s head as a long brown stalk, releasing spores to infect new hosts. While the caterpillar’s fate is grim, humans harvest these infected corpses for their perceived medicinal value, particularly in traditional Chinese and Tibetan medicine, where it’s touted as a cure for aging, cancer, and other ailments—even sold as an aphrodisiac. However, the science remains inconclusive regarding its actual health benefits. The harvesting frenzy has pushed *Ophiocordyceps sinensis* to the brink of extinction in some regions, disrupting local economies in Tibet and Nepal that rely on its trade. Conservation efforts are now underway to balance sustainable harvesting with ecological preservation.
